title: Rabies Surges 92% in Vietnam: Why the Dog Meat Trade Is a Public Health Crisis
excerpt: Vietnam recorded 34 rabies deaths and 155 animal outbreaks by mid-2026, with zero food safety oversight of the dog meat supply chain. New enforcement data reveals why unregulated slaughter poses catastrophic disease risk.
body_html:
The Bottom Line

Vietnam is facing a rabies emergency. With 34 confirmed rabies deaths through June 2026 and a 92% increase in southern Vietnam compared to 2025, health authorities are sounding alarms. But the dog meat trade remains a blind spot in food safety oversight—zero registered slaughterhouses, no traceability, and Ho Chi Minh City documented 47 food safety violations this year, including unauthorized animal slaughter and quarantine evasion. Yet 95% of Vietnamese support ending the trade.

Key Findings

Rabies Deaths Jump 92% in South Vietnam—Supply Chain Gaps Leave Citizens Exposed

Vietnam recorded 23 rabies deaths in southern Vietnam alone in the first 30 weeks of 2026, representing a dramatic spike from the same period in 2025. Nationwide, 34 deaths occurred from January through June. The crisis is compounded by a massive vaccination gap: only 42.1% of dogs and cats in Ho Chi Minh City had been vaccinated against rabies as of late July. This weak baseline is critical because rabies is nearly 100% fatal once clinical symptoms appear, making prevention the only viable public health strategy.

The dog meat trade operates entirely outside this safety net. With zero registered slaughterhouses for dog meat in Vietnam, there is no inspection, no vaccination certification, no traceability from capture to consumption. When a stolen or unvaccinated dog enters the supply chain, there is no system to detect rabies exposure before meat reaches the table—a gap that directly contradicts Vietnam's emergency rabies response.

Food Safety Violations Spike: Unauthorized Slaughter and Quarantine Evasion Detected Across Supply Chain

Ho Chi Minh City veterinary authorities reported 47 violations this year, including unauthorized animal slaughter, failures in food traceability, and quarantine evasion during transport inspections. These are not abstract regulatory gaps—they map directly onto a supply chain that moves unvaccinated, unvetted animals into kitchens and restaurants. Health authorities continue urging citizens bitten or scratched by dogs or cats to wash wounds immediately for 15 minutes with soap and water, then seek urgent medical assessment and post-exposure prophylaxis. Yet the dog meat supply chain creates precisely the conditions—no oversight, no documentation, no hygiene standards—where rabies (and E. coli, Salmonella, and other zoonotic pathogens) thrive.

95% of Vietnamese Want the Trade Ended—Public Will Aligns with Public Health Goals

The good news: a 2021 survey found 95% of Vietnamese oppose the dog meat trade, and that consensus has only hardened as health crises mount. This is not a fringe position—it is the mainstream view. What is missing is political will and enforcement infrastructure. When Hanoi approved a centralized slaughterhouse network in August 2026 for livestock and poultry, that same logic—centralization, inspection, traceability—was not extended to dog meat. The gap is glaring. A centralized, regulated dog meat supply chain (or, ideally, a ban with enforcement) would align with public health imperatives, public opinion, and the government's own animal welfare and food safety frameworks.

155 Animal Rabies Outbreaks Across 21 Provinces: The Disease Spreads Faster Than Containment

From the start of 2026 through late August, Vietnam recorded 155 animal rabies outbreaks across 123 wards and communes in 21 provinces and cities, with 282 livestock culled. This scale reveals a public health system struggling to contain a disease that thrives in conditions of poor vaccination, loose animal movement controls, and unregulated supply chains. The dog meat trade amplifies all three risk factors. Stolen dogs, strays, and uncertified animals move across province lines with no documentation. A Dong Thap rabies case in mid-August involved a stray dog that bit a sow, tested positive, and triggered quarantine measures—a pattern that repeats across the country whenever disease surveillance catches an outbreak. But many cases likely go unreported because the supply chain is invisible.

Also Worth Noting

  • Ho Chi Minh City Culled 7,400 Animals Amid Disease Outbreaks — A desperate containment measure that could have been prevented with better upstream vaccination and supply chain control.
  • Hanoi's August 2026 Centralized Slaughterhouse Network Does Not Include Dog Meat — A regulatory framework for livestock and poultry exists; the dog meat trade remains an unregulated exception.
  • Government Decree 204/2026 Imposes Rabies Fines on Dog Owners — VND 1–2 million penalties for failing to vaccinate or muzzle dogs—yet the unvaccinated dogs in the meat supply face no such enforcement.
  • Health Ministry Urges Provinces to Increase Surveillance and Post-Exposure Wound Care — A reactive posture when prevention through supply chain regulation would be far more effective.
  • Rabies Mortality Rate Remains Near 100% After Symptom Onset — This is why early detection and post-exposure prophylaxis are critical, and why unregulated meat sources pose unacceptable risk.
  • Unauthorized Slaughter and Quarantine Evasion Are Enforcement Priorities — Veterinary authorities know these gaps exist; closing the dog meat loophole is the logical next step.

Take Action: Sign the petition to support Vietnam's roadmap toward eliminating the dog meat trade by 2030 and closing a critical public health gap.
